title: When rays stop working
question: Why does the simple straight-ray picture of light fail, and what takes over?
hook: Light travelling in straight lines explains a mirror, but not what happens right at the edge of a shadow.
idea: Wave optics handles interference, diffraction and polarization, the effects that straight rays cannot describe.

beats.prompt: You trust ray-based estimates of light across a large smooth mirror. Where will those estimates be least trustworthy?

choices.label: In the middle of the mirror
choices.feedback: Away from edges the smooth surface is where the ray estimate works well.

choices.label: Everywhere equally
choices.feedback: The estimate is good for large smooth shapes; its trouble is at particular places.

choices.label: Only on surfaces that absorb light
choices.feedback: Low-reflection surfaces are actually a good fit for the method.

beats.explain: The ray-optics field is generally not accurate near edges or shadow boundaries unless diffraction calculations are added, while large smooth shapes suit it well.

beats.prompt: match each approach to what it does
pairs: Estimates a field with rays, then integrates it
Studies quantum noise in optical communication
beats.explain: Physical optics sits between ray optics and full electromagnetism; coherence theory covers effects like quantum noise that it tends to leave out.

beats.prompt: sort each case by how well the physical optics approximation suits it
items: Directions away from the mirror-like direction
beats.explain: The approximation likes big smooth shapes and high frequencies, and loses accuracy at edges, shadow boundaries and far from the specular direction.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Physical optics estimates the field on a surface using rays.
It then integrates that field over the surface.
Because it integrates, it must be an exact theory of light.
Even so, it is a standard way to estimate diffraction effects.
beats.explain: It is an approximation. The word physical only means it is more physical than ray optics, not that it is exact.
